summary: Children aged 6–7 learn that the flat faces of a 3-D solid are themselves 2-D shapes — a circle on a cylinder, triangles on a pyramid. A solid with only flat faces, such as a cube or pyramid, is built FROM those flat faces; some solids, such as a cylinder, also have a curved surface, which is not a flat face. The core teaching moves are taking solids apart (unfolding or popping up a solid so faces lie flat), tracing or paint-stamping a face to print its 2-D shape, and handling solids to feel which surfaces are flat faces and which are curved. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether drawn on paper or sitting on the solid; the whole tin is a cylinder, but each flat end is a circle.
misconceptions: Names a face by the whole solid's name — calls the flat round end of a cylinder 'a cylinder' rather than 'a circle'.
Cannot separate face from solid because the solid itself is mis-named — a cube called 'a square' has no distinct square faces to find (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023).
Sees the solid as one undifferentiated whole and does not decompose it into faces (van Hiele visual level).

activities.title: Take a solid apart into its flat faces
steps: Handle a real solid (a tin/cylinder, a cube, a square-based pyramid) and run a finger over its surfaces.
Unfold or 'pop up' a solid made from flat paper/card so its faces lie flat, then touch and count the separated faces.

Name each flattened face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) and rebuild the solid face by face. If a paper cylinder is unrolled, its curved side flattens into a rectangle, but on the cylinder that part is the curved surface, not a flat face.
State the link aloud: 'a cube is made of six squares', 'a cylinder has two circular faces and a curved surface'.
activities.insight: A solid's flat faces are 2-D shapes; a solid with only flat faces (such as a cube or pyramid) is built from them, while a cylinder also has a curved surface. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether it is drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.

activities.title: Print the face: trace and paint-stamp
steps: Dip the flat end of a tin in paint (or ink pad) and stamp it on paper; name the shape that appears.
Trace round a flat face of a cube or the square base of a pyramid and name the printed 2-D shape.
Set the printed 2-D shape beside the solid and say which face of the solid it came from.
activities.insight: The print of a solid's flat face is a plain 2-D shape (a tin's end prints a circle), making concrete that the face is itself a 2-D shape.

activities.title: Flat faces versus curved surfaces
steps: Try to rest each surface of a cylinder flat on the table: the two ends sit flat, the curved side rolls.
Sort surfaces into 'flat faces' (rest flat) and 'curved surfaces' (roll).
Count and name the flat faces on a cube, a square-based pyramid, and the cylinder; note the cylinder's side is curved, not a flat face.
activities.insight: A flat face rests flat and has a 2-D shape; a curved surface rolls and is not a flat face — so a cylinder's curved side should not be counted as a flat face.

activities.title: Decompose every face (screen peel or physical net)
steps: Rotate a solid, or its on-screen model, so faces on every side — including hidden ones — come into view.
On a screen model, peel each face off as a plain 2-D shape; with a physical solid, use an unfoldable net or pop-up so each face lies flat. Set each face beside a drawn version to compare.
Reassemble the solid from its faces and state how many of each 2-D shape it is made from.
activities.insight: Every flat face of a solid — not just the visible ones — is a 2-D shape, and a solid with only flat faces can be composed and decomposed from those flat shapes; a solid with a curved surface, such as a cylinder, also needs that curved part.

activities.title: Predict-then-stamp check
steps: Before stamping, predict and justify what shape the flat end of the tin will print.
Stamp it and compare the result with the prediction.
Match which 2-D shapes make up a given solid (e.g. two circles plus a curved surface for a cylinder) and explain the match.
activities.insight: Stating a prediction and reason in advance surfaces whether a child sees the face as a 2-D shape or conflates it with the whole solid.

checkQuestion: Run your finger over this tin (a cylinder). Point to a flat face on it — what 2-D shape is that face? Now look at this pyramid: what shape are its faces? Tell me how a face can be a 2-D shape when it is part of a solid.
checkAnswer: Identifies the flat round ends of the cylinder as circles and the faces of the pyramid as triangles (with a square base); explains that a face is the flat surface of the solid and is itself a 2-D shape, so the solid is built from 2-D faces — the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder, but each flat end is a circle.
